newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Cemex loan key part of debt overhaul.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Cemex loan key part of debt overhaul.

text.p: An announcement by Mexico's giant cement producer, Cemex SA, that its Spanish subisidary had completed a syndicated loan worth about $850 million on Wednesday finalizes a key part of the company's debt restructuring plan, analysts said.
The announcement of the deal, known about since July, is part of a complex corporate restructuring aimed at helping holding company Cemex handle its heavy debt load, they said.
Spanish subsidiary Valenciana de Cementos placed the multi-currency syndicated loan worth 108.375 billion pesetas, the biggest ever in Spain's private sector.

With the cash, Valenciana plans to buy Cemex subsidiaries Venezolana de Cementos and Sunbelt Corp, as well as restructure Valenciana's debt, including an outstanding syndicated loan, the company said in a statement.
The company said the transactions would allow it to repay debt at the holding company level. With the purchases, Valenciana will be able to funnel cash to the holding company, analysts said.

"It is a good move. The company basically needed an increase in liquidity at the holding company level, so they needed credit arrangements for managing the upstream of funds from the subsidiary to the holding company," said D.A. Campbell Co corporate analyst William Kidd.

Cemex has refinanced a good part of its debt this year, in part to meet large amounts of debt coming due over the next few years, analysts said. At the end of the third quarter, Cemex's debt stood at $4.648 billion, or 52.7 percent of its equity.
For example, in July, Cemex made a tender offer to repurchase its outstanding $1.0 billion jumbo bond due 1998 and was able to repurchase bonds equal to $541 million.
The new loan deal was also a key part of the debt overhaul.
"The only reason that people were not worried about Cemex defaulting on debt this year was because everyone assumed this loan would happen," said Salomon Bros analyst Carmen Slade.
"They have been able to refinance all of their debt and the signing of this loan is a kind of final crossing of the T on that," Slade said.
By owning more of the company's subsidiaries, Valenciana is also able to gain access to more financing, as well as having a structure to channel the money to the holding company, analysts said.

"They have also been increasing subsidiary level debt away from the holding company. At the beginning of the year not only was there too much debt maturing in the near term, there was also too much debt at the holding company, and the holding company did not have access to cash flows," Kidd said.

Santander Investments said in a recent report that with the syndicated loan, the company will be able to replace its current $171-million syndicated loan, repay a $159 million Spanish credit line, use $278 million to pay off part of the U.S. commercial paper program and/or its Bancomer credit line.

It also planned to use $64 million to retire part of the Yankee convertible debt, $105 million to reduce debt with Mexican bank Serfin, and $65 million to pay off short-term debt in Mexico, Santander said.
Cemex's stock rallied on the Mexican bolsa after the company's announcement.
"I think the stock is undervalued and I reiterated my buy a couple of days ago, but this was not why," said Slade.
One Mexico City analyst said, however, that Cemex's debt still remains too high.
"The day they announce a pre-payment of debt will be the day we take the news as favorable," said Interacciones analyst Jaime Fernandez.
